blocks.text: Vincent, and the author of De nat. rerum.

The Arabs' معرن [mʿrn] or مقرن [muqarran], i.e. horned, is without doubt the Coluber cornutus of HASSELQUIST (Travels p. 241 and 365), who described this serpent accurately. I shall set down what is most to the point: "Two tentacles (horns?), one on each side, at the sides of the crown, on the upper margin of the orbit of the eye, erect, slightly arched on the rear side and slightly channelled on the same side, somewhat hard, clothed with a tough membrane, surrounded at the base by very small scales set erect in a single row, short, half the length of the orbits of the eyes." Compare also J. D. Michaelis, Notes on the vernacular version of the Bible, on Genes. XLIX, 17. and on Numer. XXI, 6., to which passage he also added a picture of the cerastes, after the drawing that J. ELLIS inserted in the Acts of the Royal Society of London (the philosophical Transactions), December 1766. Michaelis, however, wrongly thinks that the horned snake, the cerastes of the ancients, is the same as the basilisk of the ancients, which seems rather to be the coronella, and is called by the Arabs ملكة [malika], regulus; see our note 5 on Chapter X.

Observations, book 2, ch. 55, p. 122, Paris ed. 1555, of which Paulus gave an epitome in der Sammlung der merkwürdigsten Reisen in den Orient, vol. 1 p. 206. Nor will one regret comparing what a certain learned man, expert in natural history, remarks on this passage of BELON's Observatt. in the Notes appended to the second Part of Paulus's Collection, p. 258. Bruce too has much on the horned cerastes in his Travels vol. 5, p. 200 ff., German trans., and also added a picture of it at Plate 41.
